title: Trial Specifications Document
text:
1 Introduction
This Trial Specifications Document (TSD) describes the design and technical details of the Management Strategy Evaluation (MSE) of North Pacific swordfish (Xiphias gladius; NSWO). It covers:
The TSD is a living document that will be updated as the MSE progresses to reflect the current state of the analysis.
For more information on the North Pacific Swordfish MSE process see the project homepage.

title: Trial Specifications Document
text:
1.1 About the NSWO MSE
The NSWO MSE is built and maintained by Blue Matter Science using the openMSE framework.
The analysis is fully reproducible, and all materials are available in the associated GitHub repository. The analysis scripts are in the analysis folder and are run in the order of their numbers.

title: 2  Operating Models
text:
2.1 OM Conditioning
The 2023 ISC stock assessment of North Pacific swordfish, which was fitted with Stock Synthesis 3 (SS3; Methot and Wetzel (2013)), was used to generate the operating models (OMs).
The assessment is a two-sex model with 4 quarterly time steps per year, covering 1975–2021. It includes 19 fishing fleets and 8 CPUE indices (Figure 2.1; Table 2.1). See the assessment report for further details on the assessment structure and assumptions.
The OMs were constructed by importing the SS3 output of each assessment run into the North Pacific swordfish MSE framework. The SS3 input files of the assessment runs are available from the WCNPOSWO-2023 repository.
The assessment runs were fitted with SS3 version 3.30.20.00, which has a bug in the calculation of spawning biomass. All runs were therefore re-run with SS3 version 3.30.23.1, using the original input files, and the OMs were constructed from the output of the re-run models. With the bug fixed, the unfished spawning biomass (\(SB_0\)) is calculated correctly; in the Base Case, \(SB_0\) is 105,070 t, compared with 99,808 t in the original assessment run.
Figure 2.1: Overview of the data used in the 2023 Base Case stock assessment.

title: 2  Operating Models
text:
2.1.1 Catch Units
In the assessment, the catch of 8 of the 19 fishing fleets is in numbers of fish (thousands), and the catch of the remaining fleets is in biomass (t). Because the total allowable catch (TAC) management advice produced by the candidate management procedures (CMPs) is in units of biomass (t), the catch of every fleet was imported in biomass, using the catch biomass predicted by SS3 for the fleets with catch in numbers.

2.1.2 Fleet Structure
To reduce run time, the 19 fishing fleets were combined into a single fleet in the operating models. The combined fleet reproduces the historical fishing mortality-at-age of the individual fleets, with selectivity, retention, and weight-at-age weighted by the fishing mortality of each fleet. This results in exactly the same fishery and population dynamics as an operating model with the 19 individual fleets. In the projection period, the relative contribution of each fleet (i.e., TAC allocation) is therefore assumed to be fixed at its recent pattern.







Figure 2.2: Total annual catch data in the Base Case OM.





2.1.3 Indices of Abundance
Table 2.1 lists the CPUE indices in the assessment. The indices that continue to the terminal year are provided to the CMPs:

the late-phase Japanese longline indices for Area 1 and Area 2 (S2 and S4);
the Chinese Taipei distant-water longline index (S5);
the US shallow-set longline index (S8) (Figure 2.3; see Chapter 5).

The early-phase Japanese longline indices (S1 and S3) end in 1993 and are not used by the CMPs.
S5 and S8 were not fitted in the Base Case assessment (lambda = 0). However, fitting all indices was found to have little effect on the estimated stock status. Therefore S5 and S8 are provided to the CMPs, together with S2 and S4, so that CMPs can be developed that use these indices.
S6, an index of recruitment, is simulated in the projections and available to the CMPs, but it is not used by them. Using S6 in the CMPs was tested during the MSE development, but it did not improve their performance, largely because it does not track the adult abundance. The indices used by the CMPs are described in Section 5.3.

title: 2  Operating Models
text:
2.2 Base Case and Sensitivity OMs
The Base Case OM (OM 00) is constructed from the Base Case of the 2023 assessment described above, and the CMPs are tuned to this Base Case OM (see Section 5.6 for details on the CMP tuning).
The 10 sensitivity OMs included in the MSE are constructed in the same way from alternative SS3 runs, and are used to evaluate the robustness of the tuned CMPs to uncertainty in the stock dynamics that is not captured by the Base Case.
The sensitivity (robustness) OMs explore two sources of uncertainty:


Life-history parameters: the sensitivity runs of the 2023 assessment with alternative natural mortality, steepness, growth, and maturity (runs 01–10; runs 05 and 06 are not included, see below).

Increasing catchability: two runs that assume the catchability of the indices of abundance has increased over time (effort creep) by 1% (run 20a) and 2% (run 20b) per year. These scenarios follow those used in the IATTC MSE for bigeye tuna in the eastern Pacific Ocean, where annual increases in longline catchability of 0%, 1%, and 2% are used to represent uncertainty in effort creep (Xu and Maunder 2026). These runs are the Base Case fitted to the indices deflated by \((1 + c)^{y - y_0}\), where \(c\) is the annual effort creep and \(y_0\) the first year of each index. The OMs are conditioned on the deflated indices, but the CMPs use the observed indices, so the indices seen by the CMPs over-estimate the increase in abundance (or under-estimate the decline) in these OMs. The effort creep applies only to the historical period.

Table 2.2 lists the 12 life-history and catchability runs and their key parameters.
Two of these runs (05 with steepness 0.99 and 06 with maximum size 10% larger) are not included in the MSE. In these models the SS3 fits estimated an implausibly large stock, with ln(R0) of 32.37 and 35.06 compared with 6.84 in the Base Case, and unfished spawning biomass of the order of \(10^{16}\) and \(10^{17}\) t. The stock in these OMs is therefore effectively unfished and unaffected by the catch.

2.2.1 Effort Creep OMs
In the effort creep OMs (20a and 20b), SS3 is fitted to indices deflated by 1% and 2% per year, i.e. the indices that would be obtained if they were standardized for an assumed increase in catchability over the time series (Figure 2.9). The same increase in catchability is assumed for all indices.
The deflated indices are equal to the observed indices in the first year of each index, and decline relative to them over time, so the effort creep runs estimate a larger decline in abundance over the period of the indices. To explain this decline with the same catch history, the stock is estimated to have started from a much higher state: SB/SB0 in 1975 is 0.59 in run 20a and 0.98 in run 20b, compared with 0.3 in the Base Case (Figure 2.8). In 2021, SB/SB0 is 0.38 in the Base Case, and 0.32 and 0.28 in runs 20a and 20b.







Figure 2.9: The indices used to condition the Base Case and the effort creep OMs. The Base Case is conditioned on the observed indices, and 20a and 20b on the observed indices deflated for an assumed increase in catchability of 1% and 2% per year from the first year of each index.

title: 3  Forward Projections
text:
3.1 Management Cycle and Data Lag
Each operating model has 100 independent simulations with stochastic samples of the log-normally distributed recruitment deviations, the observation error for the indices of abundance, and the catches in the initial projection years (see below).
The projection period covers 2022–2057, with 4 quarterly time steps per year.
The MSE assumes that the first TAC generated by the CMPs will apply in 2028, with a 3-year management cycle and a 2-year data lag.
This means that the TAC for 2028 is calculated in 2027 using data up to 2025, and the TAC is then updated every 3 years (Table 3.1).
The TAC is set for each calendar year and applies to the total catch of all fleets. Within each year, the TAC is split among the quarters in proportion to the seasonal distribution of the catch over the last 5 historical years.

title: 3  Forward Projections
text:
3.2 Initial Projection Years
The historical period of the OMs ends in 2021, the terminal year of the assessment. Because the first TAC generated by the CMPs will apply in 2028, the first 6 years of the projection period (2022–2027) are an extension of the historical period rather than years managed by the CMPs.
The catches in these interim years combine reported catches, where they are available, with assumed catches based on the recent catches of each fleet (all in t):


Reported catches are available for F3_US_WCNPO_LL_shallow_late and F9_US_WCNPO_LL_deep in 2022–2025, and for F19_WCPFC in 2022–2024.
The catches of F3 and F9 are reported in numbers of fish and are converted to biomass with the mean weight of the catch of each fleet in the last five assessment years.


Assumed catches are used for all other fleets and years, including all fleets in 2026–2027 and F19_WCPFC in 2025.
For each fleet, the catch is drawn from a lognormal distribution with the mean and coefficient of variation (CV) of the fleet’s catch over its last five years with catch data, truncated at the maximum catch over its last ten years. These catches are the historical catches of the OM (the catch biomass estimated in the corresponding SS3 run, which the OM reproduces) followed by any reported catches, so for most fleets they are the catches in 2017–2021.


The catches of the individual fleets are then combined into the total catch in each year (Table 3.2).

title: 3  Forward Projections
text:
3.3 Recruitment Deviations
Recruitment deviations are generated as autocorrelated, bias-corrected log-normal deviates around the stock-recruit relationship. For a given simulation, the (log-scale) deviation in year \(y\) is calculated as:
\[
\varepsilon_y \sim \text{TruncNormal}(\mu, \sigma_R,\ \pm 3\sigma_R)
\]
\[
x_y = \rho\, x_{y-1} + \varepsilon_y \sqrt{1-\rho^2}
\]
\[
\text{RecDev}_y = \exp(x_y)
\]
where \(\sigma_R\) is the recruitment deviation standard deviation, \(\rho\) is the lag-1 autocorrelation, and \(\mu = -0.5\sigma_R^2(1-\rho)/\sqrt{1-\rho^2}\) is a bias-correction term so that \(E[\text{RecDev}_y] = 1\) on the natural scale. Deviations are truncated at \(\pm 3\sigma_R\) (on the log scale).
\(\sigma_R\) and \(\rho\) are calculated for each OM from the recruitment deviations estimated in the corresponding SS3 run (Table 3.3).
\(\sigma_R\) is calculated from the main-period recruitment deviations (1985–2021). In the assessment, the recruitment deviations are estimated with a penalty that shrinks them toward zero, with a fixed standard deviation (the penalty \(\sigma_R\)) of 0.42 that sets how strongly the deviations are shrunk. Deviations that are poorly informed by the data are shrunk more, so the standard deviation of the estimated deviations underestimates the variability of recruitment. Following Methot and Taylor (2011), \(\sigma_R\) is therefore corrected for this shrinkage by adding the mean of the squared standard errors of the estimated deviations to their variance: \(\sigma_R = \sqrt{\operatorname{var}(\hat{\varepsilon}) + \overline{\text{SE}^2}}\). In the Base Case, the correction increases \(\sigma_R\) from 0.18 (the standard deviation of the estimated deviations) to 0.25.
\(\rho\) is the lag-1 autocorrelation of the log recruitment deviations in the years in which they are fully informed by the data, i.e., the years with full bias adjustment in the assessment (1996–2020).

title: 3  Forward Projections
text:
3.4 Observation Error for Simulated Data
The data used by the CMPs (catches and CPUE indices) are simulated from the OM with multiplicative observation error.
For catch, the observation error is conditioned on the historical fit between the OM catch and the catch data. The catch in the OMs matches the catch data, so the catch data provided to the CMPs match the catches in the OM (i.e., there is no observation error on the catches).
For the CPUE indices, the observation error is conditioned on the residuals between the observed index and the corresponding vulnerable abundance in the OM, including the lag-1 autocorrelation of the residuals. The index observation error in the projection period follows the same truncated, autocorrelated log-normal process described above for the recruitment deviations, continuing from the last historical residual. All indices are assumed to be proportional to vulnerable abundance (i.e., no hyperstability or hyperdepletion).
Indices are simulated in the projection period only if they have data at the end of the historical period. Table 3.4 shows the standard deviation and lag-1 autocorrelation of the observation error for these indices in the Base Case OM. The conditioned values vary among the OMs, since each OM is conditioned on its own historical fit.

title: 4  Performance Metrics
text:
4.1 Management Objectives
The CMPs are evaluated against the candidate management objectives specified in the candidate inputs for the MSE (WCPFC 2026, Attachment 7, Table 1) (Table 4.1):
The CMPs are tuned in the Base Case OM to maximise the mean annual catch subject to the Safety objective (probability of at least 0.8) and the Status objective (probability of at least 0.5 against the F target of the HCR of the CMP; Section 5.6). The Stability and Yield metrics are not used in the tuning; the trade-off between TAC stability and catch is shown by the two TAC change limits of each CMP.

title: 4  Performance Metrics
text:
Safety: Maintain spawning biomass above the limit reference point (LRP; 17% \(SB_0\)) with at least 80% probability.
Status: Maintain fishing mortality at or below the target reference point with at least 50% probability. The candidate target reference points are F\(_{40\%}\), F\(_{35\%}\), F\(_{30\%}\), the F targets of the HCRs (Section 5.2). Status is evaluated against the F target of the HCR of each CMP, and is also reported against each of the candidate target reference points. Following the advice of the ISC that the Status indicator should incorporate biomass as well as fishing mortality (WCPFC 2026, para. 46), the probability that spawning biomass is above each of the candidate threshold reference points (35%, 30%, 25% \(SB_0\)) is also reported with the Status metrics.
Stability: Changes in the TAC between management periods should be relatively gradual.
Yield: Maintain catches above average historical catch levels.

title: 4  Performance Metrics
text:
4.2 Primary Performance Metrics
All performance metrics are calculated over the 30 years in which the CMPs set the TAC (2028–2057), for each OM and CMP, from the true spawning biomass, fishing mortality, and catch in the OM (not the CMPs’ estimates). Spawning biomass and fishing mortality are averaged over the quarters of each calendar year, and catch is summed. The following notation is used:


\(s = 1, \ldots, S\) indexes the simulations and \(y \in \mathcal{Y}\) the \(N_Y\) = 30 years;

\(SB_{s,y}\) is the annual female spawning biomass, \(SB_0\) the equilibrium unfished spawning biomass, and \(SB_{\text{MSY}}\) the spawning biomass at MSY;

\(F_{s,y}\) is the annual apical fishing mortality;

\(C_{s,y}\) is the annual catch (total removals of all fleets, in t);

\(\text{TAC}_{s,c}\) is the TAC set in management cycle \(c = 1, \ldots, N_C\), and \(\Delta_{s,c} = \lvert \text{TAC}_{s,c} - \text{TAC}_{s,c-1} \rvert / \text{TAC}_{s,c-1}\) is the relative change in the TAC;

\(\mathrm{I}(\cdot)\) is 1 if the condition is true and 0 otherwise.

Safety: the probability that spawning biomass is above the LRP in any given year:
\[
P_{\text{Safety}} = \frac{1}{S N_Y} \sum_{s} \sum_{y} \mathrm{I}\left(SB_{s,y}/SB_0 > 0.17\right)
\]
Status: the probability that fishing mortality is at or below the F target, and the median ratio of the F target to fishing mortality:
\[
P_{\text{Status}} = \frac{1}{S N_Y} \sum_{s} \sum_{y} \mathrm{I}\left(F_{s,y} \leq F_{\text{target}}\right)
\]
\[
\frac{F_{\text{target}}}{F} = \frac{1}{S} \sum_{s} \operatorname*{median}_{y} \left(\frac{F_{\text{target}}}{F_{s,y}}\right)
\]
where \(F_{\text{target}}\) is the F target of the HCR of the CMP (F\(_{40\%}\), F\(_{35\%}\), F\(_{30\%}\)), the apical fishing mortality that reduces the female spawning potential ratio to the target level. \(F_{\text{target}}\) is calculated for each OM and simulation, relative to \(F_{\text{MSY}}\), in the last year with both reference points, and the annual \(F/F_{\text{target}}\) is calculated from the annual \(F/F_{\text{MSY}}\).
The probability that spawning biomass is above a threshold reference point (ThRP) is also reported with the Status metrics, for each of the candidate ThRPs (35%, 30%, 25% \(SB_0\)):
\[
P_{\text{SB > ThRP}} = \frac{1}{S N_Y} \sum_{s} \sum_{y} \mathrm{I}\left(SB_{s,y}/SB_0 > \text{ThRP}\right)
\]
Like the other metrics, this is calculated from the true spawning biomass in the OM. The same ThRPs are used for every CMP, so the metric does not depend on the ThRP of the HCR of the CMP, and CMPs with different HCRs can be compared against the same thresholds.
Stability: the probability that the TAC changes by no more than 10% between management cycles, and the probability of no management change, i.e. that the TAC changes by no more than 1% (the CMPs leave the TAC unchanged when the change would be less than 1%):
\[
P_{\text{Stability}} = \frac{1}{S N_C} \sum_{s} \sum_{c} \mathrm{I}\left(\Delta_{s,c} \leq 0.1\right)
\]
\[
P_{\text{No change}} = \frac{1}{S N_C} \sum_{s} \sum_{c} \mathrm{I}\left(\Delta_{s,c} \leq 0.01\right)
\]
Because the TAC change limit of the CMPs is either 10% or larger, \(P_{\text{Stability}}\) is 1 for the CMPs with a 10% limit.
Yield: the probability that the annual catch is at least the mean historical catch in the reference years (\(\bar{C}_{\text{ref}}\), from the OM), for two reference periods (2008–2010 and 2016–2021), and the mean annual catch:
\[
P_{\text{Yield}} = \frac{1}{S N_Y} \sum_{s} \sum_{y} \mathrm{I}\left(C_{s,y} \geq \bar{C}_{\text{ref}}\right)
\]
\[
\bar{C} = \frac{1}{S N_Y} \sum_{s} \sum_{y} C_{s,y}
\]

title: 4  Performance Metrics
text:
4.3 Secondary Performance Metrics
Status against each candidate target reference point: \(P_{\text{Status}}\) and \(F_{\text{target}}/F\) are also calculated for each of F\(_{40\%}\), F\(_{35\%}\), F\(_{30\%}\), for every CMP, so CMPs with different HCRs can be compared against the same target.
Probability that SB is above the ThRP of the HCR: \(P_{\text{SB > ThRP}}\) calculated with the ThRP of the HCR of each CMP, i.e. the proportion of years in which the true stock status is above the point where the HCR starts to reduce fishing (Section 5.2).
Probability of no breach of the LRP: the probability that spawning biomass remains above the LRP in every year; a simulation in which spawning biomass falls below the LRP in any year is a breach:
\[
P_{\text{No breach}} = \frac{1}{S} \sum_{s} \mathrm{I}\left(\min_{y \in \mathcal{Y}} SB_{s,y}/SB_0 > 0.17\right)
\]
Average TAC variability: the mean absolute relative change in the TAC between management cycles:
\[
\text{AAVY} = \frac{1}{S N_C} \sum_{s} \sum_{c} \Delta_{s,c}
\]
Kobe green quadrant: the probability that the stock is not overfished and overfishing is not occurring:
\[
P_{\text{Kobe}} = \frac{1}{S N_Y} \sum_{s} \sum_{y} \mathrm{I}\left(\frac{SB_{s,y}}{SB_{\text{MSY}}} > 1 \ \text{and} \ \frac{F_{s,y}}{F_{\text{MSY}}} < 1\right)
\]
Stock status: the mean \(SB/SB_0\), the lowest annual \(SB/SB_0\), and the mean \(SB/SB_{\text{MSY}}\) and \(F/F_{\text{MSY}}\).
Relative yield: the mean annual catch relative to the CMP with the highest mean annual catch in the same OM.

title: 4  Performance Metrics
text:
4.4 Time Windows
Safety, mean catch, and mean \(SB/SB_0\) are also calculated for three time windows:

Short: the first 10 years (2028–2037);
Medium: the years between the short and long windows (2038–2047);
Long: the last 10 years (2048–2057).

The metrics calculated over all 30 years can hide differences in when the outcomes occur. The windows show how the outcomes change over the projection period:


Safety shows when the risk to the stock occurs. For example, a CMP can meet the Safety objective over the whole period while most of the years below the LRP occur early or late in the period.

Mean catch shows how the catch is distributed over time. For example, it distinguishes CMPs with high initial catches that decline later from CMPs with lower initial catches that increase.

Mean \(SB/SB_0\) shows the trajectory of the stock, i.e., whether it is rebuilding, stable, or declining under each CMP.

title: 5  Candidate Management Procedures
text:
5.1 The Management Cycle
The MSE includes three types of candidate management procedures (CMPs):
Each CMP type is combined with each of the 6 candidate harvest control rules (HCRs; Section 5.2) and 2 limits on the change in the TAC between management cycles (10% and 20%; Section 5.5), for a total of 36 CMPs (Table 5.1). All CMPs use the same 4 indices of abundance (S2, S4, S5, S8; Section 5.3).
During development, the CMPs were tested with four sets of the available indices: the Japanese late longline indices alone (S2, S4), the Japanese indices with the US shallow-set index (S2, S4, S8), the Japanese indices with the Taiwanese index (S2, S4, S5), and all 4 indices. The choice of index set made little difference to the performance of the CMPs in these runs. To avoid presenting 144 CMPs, the set with all 4 indices was used because it uses all the available information and makes the TAC less dependent on the CPUE series of any single fleet.
Each CMP is named by its type, HCR, and TAC change limit; e.g., IR_H2_10 is the Index Rate CMP with HCR 2 and a 10% limit on the change in the TAC.
All CMPs set a single annual TAC for the total catch (removals, in t) of all fleets, which is split among the fleets and quarters in proportion to their recent catch (Chapter 3). The CMPs use data aggregated to calendar years: annual catches (summed over the quarters) and annual indices (averaged over the quarters with data). The TAC is calculated every 3 years, with a 2-year data lag (Chapter 3), and is constant within each management cycle.
In each management cycle, the CMPs follow the same sequence of steps:
The steps differ among the CMP types, and are described in full in Section 5.4.1, Section 5.4.2, Section 5.4.3, and Section 5.5.

title: 5  Candidate Management Procedures
text:
Data: the TAC is calculated in the year before the management cycle starts, from the catch and index data up to 2 years before that (e.g., the data up to 2025 for the TAC calculated in 2027 for 2028–2030; Table 3.1).

Stock status: the CMP estimates the current stock status, either from the indices relative to their level at \(SB_0\) (Index Rate and Index Target) or from the fitted surplus production model (Surplus Production).

HCR: the estimated stock status determines the HCR multiplier, which reduces the fishing intensity (or catch) when the estimated status is below the threshold reference point (ThRP).

Trial TAC: the multiplier is applied to a quantity specific to each CMP type (a catch/index rate, a reference catch, or \(F_{\text{MSY}}\)), scaled by the tuning parameter, to give a trial TAC.

TAC change limit: the change from the previous TAC is limited to the TAC change limit of the CMP, and the TAC is left unchanged if the change would be less than 1%.

title: 5  Candidate Management Procedures
text:
5.2 Harvest Control Rules
The candidate HCRs (Table 5.2) are defined in terms of stock status, \(SB/SB_0\), where \(SB_0\) is the equilibrium unfished spawning biomass, and fishing mortality (WCPFC 2026, Attachment 7, Table 2):

above the threshold reference point (ThRP), fishing mortality is at the target, \(F_{\text{target}}\);
between the ThRP and the limit reference point (LRP; 17% \(SB_0\)), fishing mortality decreases linearly from \(F_{\text{target}}\) to a minimum level, \(F_{\text{min}}\);
at and below the LRP, fishing mortality is \(F_{\text{min}}\).

\(F_{X\%}\) is the fishing mortality that reduces the spawning potential ratio to \(X\%\). \(F_{\text{min}}\) is \(F_{90\%}\) for all HCRs.

None of these quantities are observed by the CMPs, which only have the catch and the indices of abundance. The CMPs therefore use the shape of each HCR, but the HCR is applied to estimated quantities and its output is not directly a fishing mortality.

The fishing mortality that results in the OM therefore depends on how well the estimated stock status (from the indices or the surplus production model) and the TAC match the true state of the stock, and can differ from the fishing mortality intended by the HCR.

5.2.1 HCR Multiplier
In all CMPs, the output of the HCR is a multiplier, \(\theta(x)\), calculated from the estimated stock status, \(x\):
\[
\theta(x) =
\begin{cases}
\phi & x \le \text{LRP} \\[4pt]
\phi + (1 - \phi)\dfrac{x - \text{LRP}}{\text{ThRP} - \text{LRP}} & \text{LRP} < x < \text{ThRP} \\[4pt]
1 & x \ge \text{ThRP}
\end{cases}
\]
where \(\phi\) is the multiplier at and below the LRP:


Index Rate and Surplus Production: \(\phi = F_{\text{min}}/F_{\text{target}}\) of the HCR, the ratio of \(F_{\text{min}}\) to the F target in the per-recruit analysis of the Base Case OM;

Index Target: \(\phi = F_{\text{min}}/F_{\text{target}} \times \text{LRP}/\text{ThRP}\). The multiplier is lower because it applies to a catch rather than to a fishing intensity, and the catch at a given fishing intensity is lower when the stock is smaller.

For the index-based CMPs, \(x\) is the combined status of the indices (Section 5.3.4), and the LRP and ThRP are applied to it directly. For the Surplus Production CMPs, \(x\) is the estimated \(B/B_{\text{MSY}}\) of the surplus production model, and the LRP and ThRP are converted from \(B/K\), treated as equivalent to \(SB/SB_0\), to \(B/B_{\text{MSY}}\) by dividing them by \(B_{\text{MSY}}/K\) (0.5).
The HCR multiplier, as a function of estimated stock status, is shown for each HCR and CMP type in Figure 5.1.







Figure 5.1: The HCR multiplier as a function of estimated stock status for each HCR and CMP type. The dashed line shows the LRP. The multiplier applies to the fishing intensity (Index Rate and Surplus Production) or to the catch (Index Target). For the Surplus Production CMPs, the control points are applied to the estimated B/BMSY after conversion (see text).

title: 5  Candidate Management Procedures
text:
5.3 Estimated Stock Status

5.3.1 Indices
All CMPs use the 4 indices of abundance that continue to the terminal year of the assessment:

the late-phase Japanese longline indices for Area 1 and Area 2 (S2 and S4);
the Chinese Taipei distant-water longline index (S5);
the US shallow-set longline index (S8).

S5 and S8 were not fitted in the Base Case assessment (lambda = 0), but are simulated in the projections with observation error conditioned on their fit to the OM, as are S2 and S4 (Chapter 3). In the index-based CMPs (Index Rate and Index Target), the indices are equally weighted (Section 5.3.4). In the Surplus Production CMPs, the indices have equal likelihood weights, but their influence on the fit depends on their estimated observation error (Section 5.4.3).

5.3.2 Index Level at \(SB_0\)

To apply the HCR control points, which are defined in units of \(SB/SB_0\), each index \(j\) is expressed relative to its level at \(SB_0\), \(I_{0,j}\).
\(I_{0,j}\) is calibrated on the Base Case OM:
\[
I_{0,j} = \operatorname*{median}_{s} \left( \frac{\bar{I}_{j,s}}{\overline{SB/SB_0}_{s}} \right)
\]
where \(\bar{I}_{j,s}\) is the mean of the simulated index \(j\), including observation error, in simulation \(s\), and \(\overline{SB/SB_0}_{s}\) is the mean \(SB/SB_0\) in the same years. \(I_{0,j}\) is calculated once, from the Base Case OM, and used with every OM.

5.3.3 Current Status of Each Index
The current status of each index, \(S_j\), is the index averaged over the most recent RecentYears years of data (ignoring missing values), after optional loess smoothing. Both settings were selected for each index-based CMP type in Step 1 of the tuning procedure (see Section 5.6.1).
The selected values are:


Index Rate: RecentYears = 3 and Smooth = FALSE;

Index Target: RecentYears = 1 and Smooth = FALSE.

5.3.4 Combined Stock Status
Both index-based CMP types (Index Rate and Index Target) combine the indices into a single estimate of stock status, \(x\), as the mean of the status of each index relative to its level at \(SB_0\):
\[
x = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{j=1}^{n} \frac{S_j}{I_{0,j}}
\]
where \(n\) is the number of indices (4).

title: 5  Candidate Management Procedures
text:
5.4 Technical Description of CMPs

5.4.1 Index Rate
The Index Rate CMPs set the TAC as a catch/index rate multiplied by the current status of each index, in five steps:


Calibration. Each index \(j\) is calibrated into its own catch/index rate, \(\hat{r}_j\): the mean total catch over the last 2 historical years divided by the mean of index \(j\) over the same years. The calibration is done once, from the historical data (2020–2021), and is the same in every management cycle: \[
\hat{r}_j = \frac{\bar{C}_{\text{hist}}}{\bar{I}_{\text{hist},j}}
\]


Stock status. The current status of each index, \(S_j\), and the estimated stock status, \(x\), are calculated as described in Section 5.3.

HCR. The HCR multiplier, \(\theta(x)\), is calculated from the estimated stock status (Section 5.2.1).

Trial TAC. Each index’s catch/index rate is scaled by the tuning parameter, \(m\), and the HCR multiplier, and multiplied by the current status of that index, giving the TAC implied by each index. The trial TAC is the mean over the indices: \[
\text{TrialTAC} = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{j=1}^{n} S_j \times m \times \hat{r}_j \times \theta(x)
\] Because the catch/index rate is calibrated to the recent catch, \(m\) = 1 with \(\theta\) = 1 sets a TAC equal to the calibration catch when the indices are at their calibration level.

TAC change limit. The TAC change limit is applied (Section 5.5).

The fishing intensity of the Index Rate CMPs is therefore constant (apart from the HCR) and the TAC follows the indices: an increase in the indices increases the TAC in proportion.

5.4.2 Index Target
The Index Target CMPs set the TAC as a target catch (the reference catch scaled by the tuning parameter), reduced when the estimated stock status is below the ThRP, in five steps:


Reference catch. The reference catch, \(\bar{C}\), is the mean total catch over the last 5 historical years (2017–2021), and is the same in every management cycle.

Stock status. The current status of each index, \(S_j\), and the estimated stock status, \(x\), are calculated as described in Section 5.3.

HCR. The HCR multiplier, \(\theta(x)\), is calculated from the estimated stock status, with the \(\phi\) of the Index Target CMPs (Section 5.2.1).

Trial TAC. The trial TAC is the reference catch, scaled by the tuning parameter, \(m\), and the HCR multiplier: \[
\text{TrialTAC} = m \times \bar{C} \times \theta(x)
\]


TAC change limit. The TAC change limit is applied (Section 5.5).

The Index Target CMPs are therefore a constant-catch type of CMP. When the estimated stock status is above the ThRP, the trial TAC does not depend on the level of the indices: it is a fixed target catch, \(m \times \bar{C}\), which is also the maximum TAC of the CMP. The TAC moves to the target catch, within the TAC change limit, and then stays there.
The indices are used only to reduce the TAC when the estimated stock status falls below the ThRP. Because \(m\) is tuned, the target catch is not the same as the reference catch: the tuned \(m\) of the Index Target CMPs is 1.14–1.39, so their target catch is 14%–39% above \(\bar{C}\).
In contrast, the TACs of the Index Rate and Surplus Production CMPs follow the indices or the estimated biomass at all levels of stock status.

5.4.3 Surplus Production
The Surplus Production CMPs fit a Schaefer surplus production model to the annual catch and the 4 indices.
The estimated parameters are \(F_{\text{MSY}}\), MSY, and the initial depletion (\(B/K\)) at the start of the first fitted year. The carrying capacity, \(K\), follows from \(F_{\text{MSY}}\) and MSY (\(K = 2\,\text{MSY}/F_{\text{MSY}}\) for the Schaefer model), and the biomass in each later year is calculated from the initial depletion, \(K\), the productivity, and the observed catches. The biomass in the last data year is projected to the start of the management cycle (see below), and the resulting \(B/B_{\text{MSY}}\) is the estimated stock status used in the HCR.
The catch and indices contain little information on the size of the stock as the catch has been nearly constant since 1975, and the indices have no strong trend or contrast. With biomass fixed at \(K\) at the start of the catch series, the estimates of MSY and \(K\) ran to their upper bounds and most fits failed. The model is therefore:

fitted from 1994, the start of the late-phase Japanese longline indices (the early-phase indices, S1 and S3, end in 1993 and are not used), to the last data year;
fitted with the depletion in 1994 estimated (starting value 0.5);
fitted with weakly informative lognormal priors on \(F_{\text{MSY}}\) (median 0.2, CV 2), depletion in 1994 (median 0.5, CV 0.5), and MSY (median 25,737 t, twice the mean historical catch, CV 1).

The Surplus Production CMPs set the TAC from the estimated \(F_{\text{MSY}}\) and stock status, in five steps:


Model fit. The model is fitted to the catch and index data available in the management cycle. Each fit starts from the estimates of the previous management cycle. If the fit fails or does not converge, the previous TAC is kept.

Stock status. The fitted model is projected from the last data year to the start of the first year of the management cycle, with the catch in the intervening years equal to the TAC in force. The estimated stock status, \(x = \hat{B}/\hat{B}_{\text{MSY}}\), is the projected biomass relative to \(\hat{B}_{\text{MSY}}\) at the start of the management cycle.

HCR. The HCR multiplier, \(\theta(x)\), is calculated from the estimated stock status, with the control points converted to \(B/B_{\text{MSY}}\) (Section 5.2.1).

Trial TAC. The fishing mortality is the estimated \(F_{\text{MSY}}\), scaled by the tuning parameter, \(m\), and the HCR multiplier: \[
F = m \times \hat{F}_{\text{MSY}} \times \theta(x)
\] The model is projected at \(F\) for the 3 years of the management cycle, and the trial TAC is the mean annual catch of this projection.

TAC change limit. The TAC change limit is applied (Section 5.5).

The fishing mortality of the Surplus Production CMPs is therefore constant relative to the estimated \(F_{\text{MSY}}\) (apart from the HCR), and the TAC follows the estimated biomass.
In the projections, the surplus production model converged in at least 96.9% of the model fits (simulations × management cycles) for every Surplus Production CMP and OM.

title: 5  Candidate Management Procedures
text:
5.5 TAC Change Limits
For all CMPs, the proportional change from the previous TAC is limited to 10% or 20% (the TAC change limit of each CMP), both up and down, and changes smaller than 1% leave the TAC unchanged. With \(R = \text{TrialTAC}/\text{TAC}_{\text{prev}}\), the ratio of the trial TAC to the previous TAC:
\[
\text{TAC} = \text{TAC}_{\text{prev}} \times
\begin{cases}
1 & \lvert R - 1 \rvert < 0.01 \\[4pt]
1 - \delta & R < 1 - \delta \\[4pt]
1 + \delta & R > 1 + \delta \\[4pt]
R & \text{otherwise}
\end{cases}
\]
where \(\delta\) is the TAC change limit and \(\text{TAC}_{\text{prev}}\) is the TAC in force. In the first management cycle (2028), \(\text{TAC}_{\text{prev}}\) is the total catch in the last data year.

title: 5  Candidate Management Procedures
text:
5.6 Tuning Methodology
Each CMP has a single tuning parameter, \(m\), that scales the quantity to which the HCR multiplier is applied: the catch/index rate (Index Rate), the reference catch (Index Target), or \(F\) relative to \(\hat{F}_{\text{MSY}}\) (Surplus Production).
Each CMP is tuned in the Base Case OM to maximise the mean annual catch over 2028–2057, subject to the Safety and Status objectives (Chapter 4):


Safety: the probability that spawning biomass is above the LRP (17% \(SB_0\)) in any given year is at least 0.8;

Status: the probability that fishing mortality is at or below the \(F_{\text{target}}\) of the HCR of the CMP (\(F_{40\%}\), \(F_{35\%}\), or \(F_{30\%}\)) is at least 0.5.

Both probabilities are calculated from the true spawning biomass and fishing mortality in the OM, over all simulations and years.
The tuning is done in two steps.

5.6.1 Step 1: CMP Settings
The settings of the index-based CMPs that are not set by the HCR or the tuning parameter were selected from a set of candidate values (Table 5.4), using one CMP of each type: HCR 2 and a 10% TAC change limit.
Each configuration was projected at 5 values of \(m\) over 0.25–4, using the first 50 simulations, and the catch at the largest value of \(m\) that meets both constraints was interpolated. The 2 configurations with the highest catch were then fully tuned (Step 2) on all simulations, and the configuration with the highest catch was selected. The selected settings were then used for all CMPs of that type.

5.6.2 Step 2: Tuning Parameter
\(m\) was then tuned for each CMP. It was first evaluated on a grid of 7 log-spaced values over 0.25–4, which was extended if necessary, and then refined towards the largest value that meets both constraints (or the value with the highest catch, if that is lower), until the range of \(m\) is within 1% or the binding constraint is within 0.005 of its minimum.

5.6.3 Tuning Results
All 36 CMPs were tuned successfully. For 35 CMPs, the Status constraint determined the tuned value of \(m\) (Status 0.498–0.523), and for one CMP (IR_H6_20) the mean catch reached its maximum before either constraint was binding.
Safety was not limiting for any CMP: the probability that SB > LRP was at least 0.83 for every CMP, above the minimum of 0.8.
Because the Status constraint determines the tuning, the tuned catch depends mainly on the F target of the HCR (Figure 5.2; Table 5.5). The HCRs with the same F target but different ThRPs give similar results because, in the Base Case OM, the stock is above the ThRP in most years when the CMPs are tuned to the F target (65%–99% of years, depending on the CMP), so the HCR ramp has little effect (Table 5.6).

title: 6  Presentation of Results
text:
The preliminary results of the MSE are available in the Slick app, an interactive tool for exploring the performance of the CMPs across the OMs.
To view these preliminary results, open Slick in a web browser and select North Pacific Swordfish from the Case Study drop-down menu.
The app shows the performance metrics described in Chapter 4 (Table 4.2) for every CMP and OM, and allows the CMPs to be compared with a range of plots, including time series of the stock status and catch, trade-off plots, and tables of the performance metrics.
